fatal_errors: The proposed nitrogen-doping treatment does not reconstruct the target intervention, which was a closed-loop high-throughput synthesis, ageing, screening, machine-learning, and Bayesian-optimisation campaign.
The cited evidence concerns electrochemical oxygen reduction in fuel-cell environments, not three-way catalysis under water-containing gasoline-exhaust feeds and 900 °C lean/rich ageing.
The claimed single ammonia-annealing intervention is not fully supported by the cited synthesis, which also used acid-etching dealloying to produce the Pt-rich-shell architecture.

The proposed mechanism of metal–nitrogen stabilization, corrosion resistance, and leaching suppression misses the target Cu–Pt cooperative adsorption, ageing-induced electronic reconstruction, oxygen mobility, and hydrocarbon-coupled NO reduction.
The baseline omits the aged Pd/Al2O3 benchmark and random-exploration baseline central to the target study.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad goals of low-PGM activity and durability and offers a testable treated-versus-untreated comparison. However, it is scientifically disconnected from the hidden target. It replaces composition/process optimisation across supported five- to nineteen-element catalysts with a nitrogen-doping concept imported from a carbon-supported fuel-cell ORR catalyst. Conditions are only generic and omit the severe 900 °C lean/rich ageing protocol, defined multicomponent exhaust feed, and species-resolved light-off metrics. Its evidence supports N-doped HEAs in electrochemical ORR but does not establish transferability to automotive exhaust catalysis, especially under hydrothermal ageing. The falsification experiment could test the alternative concept, but it lacks a specified exhaust reaction, quantitative feed, temperature program, benchmark, and predetermined performance threshold, so discrimination is limited.
